Michael Romanov. The founding tsar of the Romanov dynasty, he emerged from the chaos of the Time of Troubles as a compromise candidate chosen by the Zemsky Sobor. He was not the greatest tsar in the mold of Peter or Catherine, yet he was essential—he was the right leader at the right moment.

Russia in 1613 was fractured. The Time of Troubles, lasting from 1605 to 1613, had brought civil war, invasion by Poland and Sweden, and multiple false claimants to the throne. The boyar families—Godunov, Shuysky, Mstislavsky—fought for dominance. No tsar seemed legitimate or capable. The Zemsky Sobor, the Assembly of the Land, convened in 1613 to choose a new tsar. After bitter debate, they elected Michael Romanov, a minor noble of modest power and neutral politics. His election was a compromise: he was young, legitimate enough to claim descent from the Rurikid dynasty through his mother, but weak enough that the boyar families could check his power.

His early reign was guided by his father, Patriarch Filaret, a powerful churchman who became regent and helped establish Romanov legitimacy. Michael faced continuing threats: Swedish and Polish armies occupied borderlands, Cossack rebellions erupted, and boyar families schemed endlessly for power. Gradually, through patience and negotiation, he repaired the realm. He concluded treaties with Sweden in 1617 and Poland in 1618, secured the borders, and reintegrated rebellious regions. He established the principle of stable succession. After decades of usurpation and chaos, the idea of hereditary Romanov rule took root.

He recovered territory lost during the Troubles, though not all. Sweden retained some Baltic lands, and Poland held the west. He reorganized provincial administration and restored the military, transforming Russia from a fractured realm into a coherent state. He strengthened the Orthodox Church and used ecclesiastical legitimacy to shore up dynastic claims. He expanded eastward into Siberia, continuing the Cossack conquest and establishing Russian dominance from Europe to the Pacific.

His son Alexei succeeded him. The dynasty was established as hereditary and stable. His great-grandson was Peter the Great, who would transform Russia into a European power. The Romanov dynasty ruled Russia for three centuries largely because Michael gave it a stable foundation.

He represents the importance of legitimacy and stability in crisis. In chaos, the steady hand matters more than the brilliant mind. His election by the Zemsky Sobor gave the dynasty a claim to democratic legitimacy that no other European monarchy could make.
